opus-5.5.text:
I look back on my time at FAIR with a lot of gratitude, and honestly some nostalgia. When I joined, FAIR felt like a very special place, almost like an idealized academic lab with industry-scale resources. The culture was very bottom-up. Nobody told you what to work on. You could talk to people like Kaiming, Ross, Piotr, and many others just down the hall, argue about ideas, and then go build them. A lot of the work I'm proudest of came from that environment, things like ResNeXt, ConvNeXt, the self-supervised learning work, and later diffusion transformers with Bill. None of those were top-down projects. They came from curiosity and from people having the freedom to follow a hunch.

Looking at how things evolved afterward, I think it shows how much the field changed rather than anyone making obviously wrong decisions. After ChatGPT, the center of gravity in AI moved very quickly toward large-scale, product-driven, highly coordinated efforts. In that world, a loosely organized research lab where everyone pursues their own taste is harder to justify inside a big company. The pressure is to concentrate compute, align everyone on a few big bets, and ship. That's understandable, but something gets lost. FAIR's strength was open research and long-term thinking, and that kind of culture is fragile. Once it starts getting reorganized around short-term goals, it's very hard to get back.

So I have mixed feelings. I'm proud of what that version of FAIR produced, and I think its commitment to open science, like publishing papers and open-sourcing code and models, shaped the whole community, including PyTorch. At the same time, I'm a bit sad that this model of research is becoming rarer in industry. That's part of why I value being in academia now. I think universities have to carry some of that torch: doing the curiosity-driven, slightly unfashionable work that may not pay off for five years but can change how people think. If there's one lesson I took from FAIR, it's that great research comes from giving smart people freedom and trust. I try to keep that spirit alive with my own students.

fable-5.1.text:
I look back on those years very warmly, honestly. I joined FAIR right after my PhD, and it was a special environment. Yann had set it up with this very open, almost academic culture: you publish everything, you release the code, you share with the community, and you're judged by whether the work actually matters, not by whether it ships into a product next quarter. For someone like me, who wanted to do fundamental research on representation learning and architectures, that was close to ideal. I had amazing colleagues, I could spend a year on a question without justifying it every week, and the resources were far beyond what any university lab could offer.

Of course, when you look at how things evolved afterward, it's a more complicated picture. The field changed a lot. Scaling became the dominant story, and the center of gravity moved toward large models and the kind of concentrated, product-driven efforts that OpenAI and others pioneered. FAIR, which had been built around open publication and a somewhat decentralized style of research, had to adjust to that. There was a period where it felt like the lab was figuring out what it wanted to be, and some very good people left during that time. I was one of them, when I moved to NYU.

But I don't see that as a judgment on the earlier years. I think the open culture at FAIR had an enormous positive effect on the whole field. PyTorch came out of that culture. A lot of the foundational work on self-supervised learning, on detection and segmentation, on architectures that people still build on, came from that period. And in a way, Meta's later commitment to open-weight models like Llama is a continuation of the same philosophy, just at a different scale and with different stakes.

If I'm honest about what I learned, it's that research environments are fragile. The combination of freedom, talent, and resources that we had doesn't last by default; it requires leadership to keep protecting it, and it requires the broader strategy of the company to still see value in it. When those things drift apart, people notice very quickly. So my time there shaped how I think about building a research group now: I try to keep that openness and that long-horizon thinking, while being realistic that the landscape I'm operating in is very different from 2016.

astra-6.text:
I’d separate my experience there from what happened afterward. I can speak to what that period meant to me, but I’d be cautious about looking at FAIR’s later trajectory and treating it as inevitable. You can end up rewriting the past through the lens of the present.

For me, the way to assess that time is to ask: What did I learn? How did my thinking change? What did I take with me? An institution can change direction, and that doesn’t erase the value of the work or the relationships people built there.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to separate two things: what the experience meant at the time, and how you interpret it knowing what happened afterward. It’s very easy to look backward and make everything feel inevitable.

For me, the value of FAIR was the people and the freedom to explore questions that didn’t necessarily have an immediate product application. You could follow an idea, discuss it with really strong researchers, and share the work openly. That’s a valuable environment, especially when you’re developing your own taste as a researcher.

Of course, that creates a tension inside a company: how do you connect long-term, open-ended research with what the business needs? As the technology becomes more commercially important, that tension becomes more visible. But I wouldn’t let the subsequent trajectory erase the value of what happened there. An institution can change, and the research and the relationships it enabled can still matter.
